gloss: mighty one, power; these; oath, curse
summary: אֱלֹהִים, אֵל and אֱלוֹהַּ name the mighty one: one who holds power over others. Scripture sets אֵל against man and flesh (“the Egyptians are men and not אֵל, their horses flesh and not spirit”), and the idiom יֵשׁ לְאֵל יָדִי, “it is in the power of my hand”, uses the word for power itself. The title belongs above all to Yahweh, the Mighty One, but scripture also gives it to angels, to judges and to Moses acting for him, and to the gods the nations serve; Ugaritic, Phoenician, Sabaic, Akkadian, Aramaic and Arabic all have the word, ʾil or ʾilāh, for a god. אָלָה is the oath sworn under the Mighty One’s curse: Yahweh cuts it with his covenant and calls it his own, it is sworn before his altar, and he carries out the curse on the one who breaks it (Sabaic writes “curse, swear” with the same letters as its god-word). אֵלֶּה points to “these” (Phoenician, Sabaic and Ge'ez ʾl, ʾellu). The entry also keeps the fat tail אַלְיָה and the one-time verb “lament”, each with Aramaic cognates of its own, and the conditional אִלּוּ; no tie between these and the rest is shown.

words.gloss: mighty ones; the Mighty One, God

senses.definition: Yahweh, the Mighty One who creates and addresses his people, “mighty one of the mighty ones”; although the noun’s form is plural, its grammar is singular in this use.

evidence.note: אֱלֹהִים is the subject of singular בָּרָא, “created”.
Yahweh is identified as הָאֱלֹהִים, with no other besides him.
אֱלֹהֵי הָאֱלֹהִים, “mighty one of the mighty ones”, set beside הָאֵל הַגָּדֹל הַגִּבֹּר, “the great, the mighty אֵל”.

senses.definition: Beings regarded or worshipped as mighty ones by those who serve them.

evidence.note: Israel is forbidden other gods.
The people are invited to sacrifices of the women’s gods.

senses.gloss: those to whom God's word came: judges
senses.definition: Men addressed as אֱלֹהִים and sons of the Most High, set to judge, who will nevertheless die like men. Jesus, quoting the Psalm, says it called them gods because God's word came to them.

evidence.note: God stands in the assembly of God and judges among אֱלֹהִים.
“I said, You are אֱלֹהִים, and all of you sons of the Most High”; the next verse says they will die like men.
Jesus quotes Psa 82:6.
“He called them gods, to whom the word of God came.”

senses.definition: The beings a little above humanity. Hebrews, quoting the Psalm, reads them as angels.

evidence.note: Humanity is made a little lower than אֱלֹהִים.
Hebrews quotes the verse: “a little lower than the angels”.

senses.definition: A title given to a person in a representative relation, without making that person the God of Israel.

evidence.note: Moses is made אֱלֹהִים to Pharaoh, and Aaron is his prophet.

senses.gloss: a godlike being in a reported vision
senses.definition: A being described as אֱלֹהִים by the woman at En Dor. The immediate narrative reports what she says she sees, rather than defining a new class of being.

evidence.note: The woman says she sees אֱלֹהִים ascending from the earth.

senses.definition: Set after a noun, אֱלֹהִים marks it as mighty or very great: a mighty prince, mighty wrestlings, an exceedingly great city, a very great trembling.

evidence.note: The Hittites call Abraham נְשִׂיא אֱלֹהִים, “a mighty prince”, among them.
Nineveh was עִיר גְּדוֹלָה לֵאלֹהִים, “a great city to God”: three days’ walk across.
נַפְתּוּלֵי אֱלֹהִים, “mighty wrestlings”, of Rachel’s struggle with her sister.
חֶרְדַּת אֱלֹהִים, “a very great trembling”, as the earth quakes.

evidence.locator: Gen.1.1, אֱלֹהִים → θεός; Psa.82.6 (LXX 81:6), אֱלֹהִים → θεοί

words.summary: A plural of the mighty one. Used of Yahweh it takes singular grammar: he is the Mighty One, mightier than all the rest. Used of others it names those who hold power over men: angels, judges, Moses sent to Pharaoh, and the gods of the nations. After a noun it marks something as mighty, very great.

senses.definition: Point to the people or things named nearby, often introducing a list or identifying a group.

evidence.note: These are the generations of the heavens and earth.

words.summary: A plural demonstrative for people or things, not a word for deity. Its relation to the God-words is not established.

senses.gloss: the Mighty One; a mighty one
senses.definition: One who holds power, set against man and flesh: Yahweh above all, and a supposed other god.

evidence.note: I am אֵל, the God of your father.
Who has formed a god or cast an image?
“Who is like you among the אֵלִם, Yahweh?”: the plural, gods.
“The Egyptians are אָדָם and not אֵל, and their horses בָּשָׂר and not רוּחַ”: man against אֵל, flesh against spirit.
The prince of Tyre says אֵל אָנִי, “I am אֵל”, and is answered, “you are אָדָם and not אֵל”.
כִּי אֵל אָנֹכִי וְלֹא אִישׁ, “for I am אֵל and not man”.
The remnant returns אֶל אֵל גִּבּוֹר, “to the mighty אֵל”.
The child’s name includes אֵל גִּבּוֹר, “mighty אֵל”, as Yahweh is called in Isa 10:21.
לֹא אִישׁ אֵל וִיכַזֵּב, “אֵל is not a man, that he should lie”.

senses.definition: In the idiom יֵשׁ לְאֵל יָד, “it is in the power of (one's) hand”, and its negative אֵין לְאֵל יָד: the ability to carry something out.

evidence.note: Laban: “It is in the power of my hand to do you harm.”
Children given to another people, “and there is no power in your hand”.
They do evil at morning light “because it is in the power of their hand”.

senses.definition: Set after a noun, אֵל marks the mightiest of its kind: mountains and cedars “of God”, set in parallel with the great deep.

evidence.note: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of אֵל, your judgments the great deep.”
“Cedars of אֵל.”

senses.definition: In the plural, mighty ones who are not God: the mighty among the warriors in the grave, and the בְּנֵי אֵלִים called to give Yahweh glory and strength.

evidence.note: אֵלֵי גִבּוֹרִים, “the mighty among the warriors”, speak from the midst of שְׁאוֹל: men, who have died.
הָבוּ לַיַהְוֶה בְּנֵי אֵלִים, “give to Yahweh, sons of the mighty”, glory and strength.

words.summary: The mighty one, set against man, who is flesh (Isa 31:3; Ezk 28:2; Hos 11:9), and named above all of Yahweh, אֵל גִּבּוֹר, “the mighty אֵל”. In the idiom יֵשׁ לְאֵל יָדִי it is power itself, “the power of my hand”, and after a noun it marks the mightiest of its kind. The cognates all have the word for a god; none of them means “power”, so the power sense rests on scripture’s own use.

opposites.note: Man, set against אֵל: what man cannot do, אֵל can.
Flesh, the weakness of man, set against אֵל and spirit.

parallels.note: Mighty, warrior: אֵל גִּבּוֹר, “the mighty אֵל”.

senses.gloss: the Mighty One, God; a god
senses.definition: The singular divine title, frequently naming God and also used of a god worshipped by others.

evidence.note: Jeshurun abandons the God who made him.
The ruler honors a god his fathers did not know.

senses.definition: The oath by which someone binds himself, calling a curse on himself if he breaks it; often joined with a covenant, and Yahweh calls the oath he imposed “my oath”.

evidence.note: The servant can be released from Abraham’s oath.
“Let there be an אָלָה between us… let us cut a covenant with you.”
Yahweh: “my אָלָה that he despised and my covenant that he broke”.
Israel enters בִּבְרִית יַהְוֶה אֱלֹהֶיךָ וּבְאָלָתוֹ, “the covenant of Yahweh your God and his אָלָה”, which Yahweh cuts with them.
“I cut this covenant and this אָלָה”, with those present and those not yet born.
The returned exiles enter בְּאָלָה וּבִשְׁבוּעָה, “into an אָלָה and an oath”, to walk in God’s law.
The man put under an אָלָה comes “before your altar in this house”, and God hears in heaven and judges.

senses.definition: The curse pronounced or written as the sanction of an oath, and by extension an imprecation.

evidence.note: The priest writes the curses and washes them into the water.
“The oath (שְׁבֻעָה) of the curse (אָלָה)”: the curse is what the oath calls down.
The curse goes out over the land against the thief and the false swearer.
“All the אָלָה written in this book shall lie on him, and Yahweh shall blot out his name”: the curse is Yahweh’s to carry out.
“The אָלָה and the oath written in the law of Moses has been poured out on us, because we sinned against him.”
The wicked man’s mouth is full of אָלָה, “cursing”, and deceit; Paul quotes it in Rom 3:14.
“Whose mouth is full of cursing (ἀρά) and bitterness”, quoting Psa 10:7 of all who are under sin.

words.summary: The oath by which someone binds himself under the Mighty One’s curse, and the curse itself. Yahweh cuts his covenant “and his אָלָה” with Israel (Deu 29:11); the oath is sworn before his altar and he judges by it (1Ki 8:31); and he carries out the curse on the one who breaks it (Num 5:21; Deu 29:19). Sabaic has one word, written like its god-word, for “curse, swear”, and Arabic has “swear”.

parallels.note: Oath, paired with אָלָה: the sworn word and the curse that sanctions it.

senses.definition: Utter an oath or curse, sometimes falsely or wrongfully.

evidence.note: Micah’s mother has pronounced a curse concerning the stolen silver.

senses.definition: Require someone to act or answer under the sanction of an oath.

evidence.note: Saul binds the people with a curse against eating before evening.

words.summary: Swear or put someone under an oath that calls down the Mighty One’s curse on the one who breaks it. Micah’s mother pronounces the curse and then blesses her son “to Yahweh” (Jdg 17:2); the one put under oath stands before Yahweh’s altar (1Ki 8:31).

senses.definition: The fatty tail removed near the backbone and presented with the animal’s fat.

evidence.note: The whole fat tail is removed close to the backbone.

words.summary: The fatty tail of a sheep, offered with its other fat. Arabic and Aramaic have the same word for it; how it relates to the entry's other meanings is not shown.

senses.definition: Introduce a supposed situation, often one contrary to the present facts.

evidence.note: If the people had merely been sold as slaves, Esther says she would have kept silent.
Even if someone lived two thousand years without seeing good.

words.summary: Introduces a hypothetical condition, in two late passages. Aramaic has the same word (the Targums render both verses with it). It looks like a compound of a conditional particle (אִם, Aramaic אִן) with לוּ “if only”, not a word formed from this root; it is kept here by spelling.

senses.definition: A curse invoked against enemies; the noun occurs once.

evidence.note: The speaker asks for God’s curse upon them.

words.summary: A curse invoked on enemies, asked of Yahweh: “give them … your תַּאֲלָה”. Formed from the verb אָלָה.

senses.definition: Mourn in grief like a young woman bereaved of her husband.

evidence.note: The lament is compared to a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth.

words.summary: A single command to lament, fixed by its simile of a young widow in sackcloth. Aramaic has the verb “lament, wail” and a noun “wailing woman”; no tie to swearing or to deity is shown.

senses.definition: Identify a plural group already in view.

evidence.note: All these lands: הָאֲרָצֹת הָאֵל.

words.summary: A shorter demonstrative form beside אֵלֶּה, distinct from the divine noun אֵל.

senses.definition: The divine title, with singular or plural forms as required.

evidence.note: The God of heaven gives the king his kingdom.
The gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish.

senses.definition: A plural demonstrative in the Aramaic saying in Jeremiah.

evidence.note: “Under these heavens” closes the Aramaic verse.

senses.definition: The divine title used for God, or for what someone regards as a god.

evidence.note: Worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.

senses.definition: What belongs to being God, rather than an image made by human craft.

evidence.note: Divinity is not to be thought like gold, silver, or carved stone.

evidence.note: His divine power has given what is needed for life and godliness.

doctrine.statement: Deuteronomy 4:35 identifies Yahweh as God and says there is no other besides him. Paul distinguishes the many beings called gods and lords from “one God, the Father” and “one Lord, Jesus Christ” confessed by believers (1Co 8:5–6). Thus the word’s application to something worshipped does not establish that it is God in the sense affirmed of Yahweh.

Yahweh cut his covenant with Israel together with “his אָלָה”, the curse under which they bound themselves (Deu 29:11, 13). Whoever turned away would have “all the אָלָה written in this book” lie on him, and Yahweh would blot out his name (Deu 29:19). Israel broke it, and Daniel confesses that “the אָלָה and the oath written in the law of Moses” had been poured out on them because they sinned (Dan 9:11); the returned exiles bound themselves again under an אָלָה to walk in God’s law (Neh 10:30). Paul says that all who rest on the works of the law are under the curse, as “everyone who does not continue in all things written in the book of the law” (Gal 3:10, quoting Deu 27:26 in the words of Deu 29:19), and that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations (Gal 3:13–14). The curse Israel swore under is the curse Christ bore.

note:
The spelling holds words of several older roots, not one semantic origin. Proper names, including the month אֱלוּל, are left for name entries. Terebinth אֵלָה is not filed under this root in the brief (its tree-words go with אַיִל, אֵלוֹן); no claim about its root is made here. Redirects are omitted. The Hebrew short demonstrative (rootless a.dj.aa) and Aramaic אִלֵּין are included as forms of the demonstrative family. The Aramaic short אֵל (xa.an.aa) has no distinct Aramaic occurrence established here. Exo 21:6 and 22:7–8 can be read as appearing before God or before judges; they are not used to make “judges” an unqualified separate sense. Psalm 82’s אֱלֹהִים are read as Jesus reads them (Jhn 10:35), and Psa 8:6’s as Hebrews reads them (Heb 2:7); 1Sa 28:13’s reported vision still needs contextual review.

Open questions (2026-11-09): (1) The Hebrew forms themselves point to two older roots behind the spelling: אֱלוֹהַּ has a consonantal ה (mappiq), as Sabaic and Arabic ʾlh “god”, while the oath verb is third-weak (וַיֹּאֶל, אָלִית, תַּאֲלָה), as Arabic ʾlw/ʾly “swear”; the lament אֱלִי and the fat tail אַלְיָה are also ʾly. ה is not one of the merged letters the `sounds` field records, so the split shows only here. Against it, Sabaic writes “curse, swear” ʾlh with the same letters as its god-word, and Arabic إِلّ joins “God” (disputed) and “covenant”: whether the oath was first sworn by the god is open. (2) The “power” sense of אֵל (יֵשׁ לְאֵל יָדִי) and the superlative “mountains of God” may be another root (BDB's leads: אול “be strong”); no cognate meaning “power” has been found. (3) אִלּוּ looks like a compound (אִם/אִן + לוּ) rather than a word of this root; consider moving it out. (4) Not found or not checked: Ugaritic has no oath, fat-tail or lament word of this shape in Segert or Fisher; Krahmalkov has no Phoenician ʾlt “oath, curse” (the Arslan Tash amulet's ʾlt, if wanted, needs DNWSI); the Mesha stele text was not checked for ʾl; Ge'ez has no god-word of this root (አምላክ is from mlk), so none is cited; Syriac (Payne Smith) not yet consulted for the lament and fat-tail words.

Gloss change (2026-11-09, user's direction): the God-words are glossed “mighty one”, not “God”, because scripture gives the title to men and angels and sets אֵל against man and flesh (Isa 31:3, Ezk 28:2, Hos 11:9), and the idiom יֵשׁ לְאֵל יָדִי uses it for power. Against this: every cognate (Ugaritic il, Akkadian ilu, Phoenician ʾl, Sabaic ʾl/ʾlh, Arabic ʾilāh) means “god”, none “power”, so the sense rests on scripture's use alone; and the superlative uses could run either way (from “mighty” to “divine” or the reverse). Related spellings with י/ו to weigh later: אֵיל גּוֹיִם “mighty one of the nations” of Nebuchadnezzar (Ezk 31:11), אֵילֵי הָאָרֶץ “the mighty of the land” (2Ki 24:15, ketiv אולי), אֱיָלוּת “strength” (Psa 22:20), אוּל “strength” (Psa 73:4).

Oath and the Mighty One (2026-11-09, user's direction): the oath words are tied to “mighty one” by scripture's use: the אָלָה is Yahweh's (Deu 29:11), sworn before his altar (1Ki 8:31), carried out by him (Num 5:21, Deu 29:19). Formally the oath verb is third-weak (וַיֹּאֶל, אָלִית), as Arabic ʾlw “swear”, while אֱלוֹהַּ has a consonantal ה and אֵל has no third letter; Sabaic writes both ʾlh. A two-letter base ʾl extended two ways would fit, but is inference. Gal 3:10 quotes Deu 27:26 (אָרוּר), whose curse words are ארר, not this root; the doctrine ties it to אָלָה through Deu 29:19's “written in this book” and Dan 9:11's κατάρα, which Paul uses.
